credentials.credibility_notes: Randomization supports causal inference, but applicability specifically to initiation cannot be fully assessed without baseline aspirin use.

evidence.text: The trial assigned 9,525 participants to aspirin and 9,589 to placebo; 1,052 deaths occurred over a median follow-up of 4.7 years.

evidence.text: Over median follow-up of 4.7 years, all-cause mortality was higher with aspirin: 12.7 versus 11.1 deaths per 1,000 person-years, with a hazard ratio of 1.14 (95% CI 1.01–1.29). This is an overall mortality result, not a cardiovascular-specific net-benefit measure.
evidence.quote: The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29).

credentials.credibility_notes: Randomized mortality evidence is relevant to overall harm, but it does not isolate cardiovascular harm or bleeding; the authors caution that the mortality finding was unexpected.

evidence.text: Cancer-related deaths occurred in 3.1% of aspirin recipients versus 2.3% of placebo recipients, with a hazard ratio of 1.31 (95% CI 1.10–1.56); the source identifies cancer as the major contributor to excess mortality, at 1.6 excess deaths per 1,000 person-years.
evidence.quote: Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years.
